item.mechanism: The presence of chemical short-range order (SRO) creates diffuse antiphase boundaries (DAPBs) when a screw dislocation glides, requiring extra energy to break the local order, which reduces the rate of double-kink nucleation and provides strengthening.
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures from 300 K to 2000 K; shear stresses from 0 to 3.0 GPa; SRO state equilibrated at 800 K; fast timescales where SRO state does not change around the dislocation.
item.supporting_observation: At 300 K, the influence of SRO is clearly apparent; based on the shift in the velocity curve, we can estimate the extra strengthening from SRO to be ~180 MPa.
item.scope_limits: The strengthening effect is observed to attenuate at increasing temperatures; at 2000 K, the mobility in RSS and SRO samples essentially overlaps. The model assumes the effect is on kink-pair formation energy and neglects effects on kink motion.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that a classical athermal model (Fisher) predicts strengthening should be constant at higher temperatures, which contradicts the observed attenuation.
quotes: We can attribute this SRO effect to be associated with the break-up of local chemical order which creates diffuse antiphase boundaries (DAPBs).
At 300 K (Fig. 2c ), the influence of SRO is clearly apparent; based on the shift in the velocity curve, we can estimate the extra strengthening from SRO to be ~180 MPa.
Indeed, when the temperature reaches 2000 K, the dashed and solid lines in Fig. 2f , respectively, representing the screw dislocation mobility in the RSS and SRO samples, essentially overlap.

item.mechanism: A cross-slip locking mechanism occurs where screw dislocation segments move onto different slip planes, creating jogs that pin the dislocation line and require extra stress or thermal activation to unlock.
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures around 1200 K; shear stresses of 1.4 GPa (RSS) and 2.0 GPa (SRO); short dislocation line lengths (~15 nm).
item.supporting_observation: In the inset, one segment of the dislocation line has moved to the upper slip plane by cross-slip, represented by the red color, and two jogs are created at the intersections between the cross-slipped segment and the original blue segment.
item.scope_limits: Observed for short dislocation segments (~15 nm) in MD simulations; the mechanism leads to the whole dislocation line becoming immobile on the simulation timescale unless unlocked by high stress.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors distinguish these jogs from previously defined cross-kinks, noting they are somewhat more complex and involve periodic boundary conditions.
quotes: Specifically, this figure displays the screw dislocation line with periodic boundary conditions where the atoms are colored by the height of the slip planes.
Extra stress is then required for the dislocation to break or move these jogs, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 3 .
In this case, the whole dislocation line becomes immobile (on the timescale of the MD simulation) due to the pinned jogs during the entire simulation time after they form.

item.mechanism: Edge dislocation mobility is enhanced by the presence of chemical short-range order (SRO), contrasting with the reduced mobility of screw dislocations.
item.operating_conditions: Wide temperature range (implied 300-2000 K based on context); presence of SRO equilibrated at 800 K.
item.supporting_observation: The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced.
item.scope_limits: The text does not provide detailed figures or specific stress/temperature data for edge dislocations in this excerpt, only the general finding.
item.alternatives_considered: Not stated in the provided text.
quotes: The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced.
Independent of the presence of SRO, a cross-slip locking mechanism is observed for the motion of screws, which provides for extra strengthening for refractory high-entropy alloy system.

Here, we investigate mechanisms underlying the mobilities of screw and edge dislocations in the body-centered cubic MoNbTaW RHEA over a wide temperature range using extensive molecular dynamics simulations.

item.mechanism: Screw dislocation motion is governed by thermally activated kink-pair nucleation and migration, with the Gibbs free energy of formation determining the velocity in the low-temperature/low-stress regime.
item.operating_conditions: Low-to-middle temperature and stress regimes; specific temperatures 300-2000 K; shear stresses 0-3.0 GPa.
item.supporting_observation: An analysis of the atomic configurations during screw dislocation glide reveals that the dominant mechanism underlying dislocation motion... corresponds to thermally activated kink-pair nucleation and migration.
item.scope_limits: At high stress and temperature, the mechanism transitions to a phonon-drag regime where the exponential term becomes negligible.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors consider the transition to phonon drag when the free energy of kink-pair formation becomes negative or zero.
quotes: An analysis of the atomic configurations during screw dislocation glide reveals that the dominant mechanism underlying dislocation motion for the dislocation lengths and timescales probed in the lower-to-middle temperature and stress regimes, corresponds to thermally activated kink-pair nucleation and migration.

item.mechanism: The formation of cross-kinks and jogs (superkinks) is facilitated by the intrinsic fluctuation in energy along the dislocation line and the rugged energy landscape in RHEAs, making cross-slip locking more important than in pure bcc metals.
item.operating_conditions: Concentrated solid solution environment; dislocation line lengths and timescales probed in MD simulations.
item.supporting_observation: The intrinsic fluctuation in energy along the dislocation line and the rugged energy landscape for screw dislocation segments in RHEAs... can further facilitate cross-slip along the dislocation line and cause the formation of jogs.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism is specific to concentrated solid solutions where solute-dislocation interaction energy is high compared to pure metals.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors compare this to pure bcc metals or dilute binary alloys where such locking is expected to be less frequent.
quotes: This phenomenon thus provides extra strengthening and can lead to debris such as vacancies, interstitials, and prismatic loops.

item.mechanism: The strengthening effect of SRO on screw dislocations is modeled by adding an enthalpic term (ΔH_DAPB) to the Gibbs free energy of kink-pair nucleation, representing the energy cost to disrupt local order.
item.operating_conditions: SRO state fixed at 800 K; temperatures 300-2000 K; shear stresses in the kink-pair nucleation regime.
item.supporting_observation: For the RHEA with local chemical SRO, the nucleation of each kink-pair will break the local order and create a small segment of DAPB, which needs to be included in the Gibbs free-energy term.
item.scope_limits: The model assumes the effect of DAPB during kink-pair migration is small and neglects it; it also assumes the SRO state is fixed and does not evolve during dislocation motion.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors initially considered a classical athermal model (Fisher) but found it inconsistent with the temperature-dependent attenuation observed in simulations.
quotes: In so doing, we assume that the dominant effect of SRO is on the kink-pair formation energy, and neglect its effect on kink motion after formation.

item.mechanism: The simulation setup uses short dislocation line lengths (~15 nm) to focus on intrinsic mechanisms, acknowledging that calculated velocities depend on this length scale.
item.operating_conditions: MD simulations with periodic length along dislocation line of ~15 nm; temperatures 300-2000 K; shear stresses 0-3.0 GPa.
item.supporting_observation: Due to practical considerations of computation cost, the current work considers a periodic length along the dislocation line direction of ~15 nm.
item.scope_limits: The velocities are dependent on the line length employed; the study focuses on intrinsic mechanisms of short segments rather than absolute mobility magnitudes for realistic experimental conditions.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that detailed comparisons of mobility magnitude would require extrapolation to larger line length scales using theoretical models.
quotes: The simulations thus investigate the motion of dislocations with line lengths that are quite short compared with those characteristics of realistic experimental conditions and considered in theoretical models.
The velocities calculated in the current setup are expected to be dependent on length in the range of size employed in this work.
Thus, the focus in the present work is on understanding the intrinsic mechanisms underlying the motion of short dislocation segments, and the associated effects of SRO.

item.mechanism: The machine-learning interatomic potential (MTP) accurately captures the variation in dislocation core energies as a function of local environment, including systems with varying degrees of SRO.
item.system: NbMoTaW RHEA (training data includes elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems)
item.operating_conditions: Validation against DFT calculations for supercells with dislocation dipoles; training on energies and forces.
item.supporting_observation: The distribution of dislocation dipole energies obtained with the MTP is found to be in excellent agreement with these previous DFT results.
item.scope_limits: The potential was developed and validated for the specific Nb-Mo-Ta-W system; accuracy is near DFT for the training data range.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors compare the MTP to a previous spectral neighbor analysis potential (SNAP), noting the MTP has decreased force MAEs.
quotes: The distribution of dislocation dipole energies obtained with the MTP is found to be in excellent agreement with these previous DFT results, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 1.

These results suggest that the MTP provides an accurate model for the variation in dislocation core energies as a function of the local environment, motivating its use in the current MD studies of dislocation mobilities.

item.mechanism: SRO increases the formation energy of a double kink (via ΔH_DAPB), creating a temperature-dependent strengthening effect on screw dislocations that diminishes at high temperatures due to the entropy term in the free energy barrier.
item.system: MoNbTaW RHEA with chemical Short-Range Order (SRO)
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures of 300 K and 2000 K; stress regimes where screw dislocation motion is governed by double-kink nucleation (excluding cross-kink pinning); fitted model parameters based on RSS samples.
item.supporting_observation: The model shows that at high temperature (2000 K), the strengthening effect from SRO is significantly diminished compared to behavior at room temperature (300 K), consistent with MD results.
item.scope_limits: Does not hold for edge dislocations (where SRO enhances mobility); effect is specific to the kink-pair nucleation mechanism for screw dislocations; does not apply when cross-kink pinning is active.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered the standard kink-pair nucleation model without SRO (RSS case) as a baseline to isolate the SRO effect.
quotes: the strengthening effect from SRO is significantly diminished compared to behavior at room temperature (300 K)

item.mechanism: SRO flattens the energy landscape for edge dislocations, reducing the solute drag effect and enhancing mobility, which offsets the energy cost of creating a DAPB.
item.system: MoNbTaW RHEA with chemical Short-Range Order (SRO)
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures from 300 to 2000 K; stress regimes including low and high stress; edge dislocation glide in bcc metals.
item.supporting_observation: The initial relaxed edge dislocation line in the SRO sample is observed to be straighter than that in the RSS sample, implying a flatter energy landscape.
item.scope_limits: Effect is observed in the high-stress regime where the SRO on the specific slip plane is destroyed by dislocation motion, but neighboring planes retain order; does not apply to screw dislocations.
item.alternatives_considered: Previous understanding that SRO onset necessitates break-up of local order requiring extra energy (which would hinder motion) was considered and found contradictory.
quotes: the existence of SRO can also influence the solute interactions and, as such, lower the solute drag effect to enhance the mobility of the edge dislocation.
the effect of SRO in inducing a considerably flattened energy landscape (lower solute drag effect) could offset the extra energy cost to create a DAPB
the velocity of the edge dislocations is enhanced in the SRO sample compared to that in the RSS sample.

item.mechanism: The influence of SRO on edge dislocation mobility extends to neighboring atomic planes, with a characteristic length scale of approximately 1.2 nm, where randomizing these layers reduces the mobility enhancement.
item.system: MoNbTaW RHEA with chemical Short-Range Order (SRO)
item.operating_conditions: 300 K; applied shear stress of 0.6 GPa; simulations where 1, 2, or 4 layers of atoms around the slip plane were manually randomized.
item.supporting_observation: When four layers of atoms are randomized in the SRO sample, the thickness of the RSS region is 1.2 nm and the average velocity of the dislocation nearly converges to the velocity in the sample with the complete random disorder.
item.scope_limits: Effect is limited to the range of ~1.2 nm; beyond this distance (or when all layers are randomized), the SRO enhancement vanishes.
item.alternatives_considered: The possibility that SRO only affects the specific slip plane was considered, but the data showed influence from neighboring planes.
quotes: this result supports our hypothesis that SRO would reduce the solute drag interaction for the edge dislocation
shows that this effect extends to a characteristic length scale of ~1.2 nm.

item.mechanism: In pure bcc metals, edge dislocations exhibit no threshold stress (friction) because they are not subject to solute drag, whereas in RHEAs, solute drag interactions create a temperature-dependent friction stress.
item.system: MoNbTaW RHEA (RSS) compared to pure Mo and pure Nb
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures of 300 K and 2000 K; stress ranges from 0 to 1.0 GPa; edge dislocation motion.
item.supporting_observation: The most notable difference in this comparison is that there is no threshold stress effect in the pure metals, associated with solute drag.
item.scope_limits: Does not apply to screw dislocations in pure metals, which still exhibit friction due to kink-pair nucleation barriers; specific to the presence of solute atoms in RHEAs.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered the standard behavior of pure metals where edge dislocations glide freely without solute drag.
quotes: there is no threshold stress effect in the pure metals, associated with solute drag.
due to solute drag interactions we can clearly observe temperature-dependent friction stress for the edge in the RHEA
the friction is zero in pure metals for edge dislocations, whereas due to solute drag interactions we can clearly observe temperature-dependent friction stress for the edge in the RHEA

item.mechanism: The critical friction stress for screw dislocations decays exponentially with temperature due to the lowering of the free-energy barrier for kink-pair nucleation, while for edge dislocations it decays linearly due to solute drag.
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures from 300 to 2000 K; stress regimes determining critical friction stress (velocity thresholds of 0.2 Å/ps for screw, 1.0 Å/ps for edge).
item.supporting_observation: The critical stress for the screw dislocation is more sensitive to the increment of temperature and, as such, decays at a much higher rate compared with the edge dislocation.
item.scope_limits: This distinct difference in temperature sensitivity is found only in the RHEA, not in elemental bcc metals where both mechanisms behave differently.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered the behavior in binary alloys (Mo-Nb) which showed lower friction stresses but similar trends to pure metals.
quotes: critical stress as a function of temperature for the screw dislocation in RSS samples obtained from MD simulations (open symbols), fitted with an exponential function
the critical stress for the edge dislocation is well fit by a function that decreases linearly with temperature.
from 300 to 2000 K the critical friction stress decreases by 140 MPa for the edge dislocation, whereas the decrease is almost an order of magnitude larger at 1.3 GPa for the screw dislocation.

item.mechanism: The ratio of edge-to-screw mobility decreases with increasing temperature in both pure bcc metals and RHEAs, as screw dislocation velocity increases (due to lower kink-pair barriers) while edge dislocation velocity decreases (due to phonon drag).
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures of 300 K and 2000 K; stress regimes for double-kink mechanism (screw) and solute drag/phonon drag (edge).
item.supporting_observation: The edge-to-screw mobility ratio is around 20 at 300 K, which decreases to 11 when the temperature is raised to 2000 K.
item.scope_limits: The ratio decreases in both RHEAs and pure metals, indicating it is not a unique feature of RHEAs, though the absolute values differ.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors noted discrepancies with other systems (CoFeNiTi) potentially due to different lattice distortion levels.
quotes: the mobility of the edge dislocations does decrease with increasing temperature due to phonon drag
the velocity of the screw dislocations moving by a double-kink mechanism is found to increase with temperature due to a lowering of the free-energy barrier for kink-pair nucleation.
The ratio of the edge-to-screw velocities does indeed decrease as the temperature is raised

item.mechanism: SRO induces a flattened energy landscape for screw dislocation cores, which is assumed to be relevant for edge dislocations as well, contributing to the reduction of solute drag.
item.operating_conditions: Ground state/relaxed configurations; comparison between RSS and SRO samples; edge and screw dislocation cores.
item.supporting_observation: our previous DFT study showed a flattened energy landscape for the screw dislocation cores in the RHEA due to the presence of SRO, which can be assumed also to be of relevance to edge dislocations.
item.scope_limits: The flattening for edge dislocations is an assumption based on screw dislocation DFT results; the effect is specific to the presence of SRO.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered the standard rugged energy landscape of RSS samples which leads to higher solute drag.
